extraction.name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
extraction.description: A comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. It comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories, including natural sounds, music, spoken dialogue, multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and heterogeneous images.
extraction.creator: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li
extraction.citeAs: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li. VOICEASSISTANT-EVAL: BENCHMARKING AI ASSISTANTS ACROSS LISTENING, SPEAKING, AND VIEWING. arXiv:2509.22651v1, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was collected by extracting diverse visual and auditory inputs from source datasets and converting text instructions into spoken prompts. The dataset is organized into three subsets: Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. Listening data were collected from 23 audio understanding datasets and include sounds, music, speech, and general audio. Speaking data were built from 22 datasets plus role profiles and question texts from RoleBench, with all interactions voice-driven and requiring spoken responses. Viewing data were sourced from MMMU and paired with audio tasks. For role-play, the authors selected 100 distinct roles and collected three representative audio clips per role. They synthesized speech instructions using three TTS models, evaluated generated speech with UTMOS, transcribed it with Whisper, and retained recordings with the lowest word error rates. A multi-stage curation process included deduplication, validation, categorization, and balanced sampling.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source data come from 47 datasets in total. Listening uses 23 audio understanding datasets; Speaking uses 22 datasets including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets, plus RoleBench for role profiles and question texts; Viewing uses MMMU as the source dataset. The benchmark includes extracted audio clips, images, role audio clips, and synthesized spoken question audio.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors converted collected text instructions into audio, replaced image reference tokens with descriptive phrases, rewrote text for TTS readability using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, rephrased multiple-choice options for readability, regenerated low-quality synthesized clips until UTMOS exceeded 3.8, transcribed synthesized audio with Whisper-Large-v3, selected samples with the lowest word error rate, de-duplicated content using lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance with manual review, removed incomplete or inappropriate items, assigned items to 13 task categories, and applied balanced sampling to equalize category representation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included converting text instructions to spoken prompts; replacing special image tokens such as "<image1>" with descriptive phrases; rewriting text to improve TTS quality and pronunciation of numbers and mathematical expressions; rephrasing multiple-choice options for readability; evaluating synthesized speech with UTMOS Strong and regenerating clips scoring below 3.8; transcribing synthesized audio back into text with Whisper-Large-v3 and selecting the sample with the lowest word error rate; deduplicating questions; filtering corrupted images, silent or broken audio, ill-posed prompts, incorrect answers, and other incomplete or unsuitable instances; categorizing remaining items; and balanced sampling.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper describes manual curation and validation rather than conventional labeling. Curators reviewed candidate items in a web-based curation tool and assigned a Good or Bad verdict with optional notes. Manual review proceeded in three passes: media integrity, task well-posedness, and answer validity. For role-play evaluation, speaker similarity was computed against reference role audio. The paper also describes evaluator prompts used to assess model outputs, but these are for benchmark evaluation rather than dataset item annotation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Suspected duplicates identified by lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance were manually reviewed and removed. The curation tool exported an audit log with item IDs, curator decisions, and timestamps. Approximately 10% of candidates were discarded during validation. For synthesized speech, the authors evaluated outputs with UTMOS and Whisper word error rate, regenerating or selecting clips based on these scores.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, F5-TTS, ChatTTS, Dia-1.6B, UTMOS Strong, Whisper-Large-v3, Wespeaker
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that they will release both the dataset and evaluation code. They will maintain a data governance process for auditing and removal and reserve the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise. They also mention providing safety cards describing acceptable use, known risks, and red-team tests for voice cloning abuse.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker voices and role audio clips are included for role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation. The paper also mentions user emotions in the Speaking subset and notes five Chinese roles in the role-play task, while all other prompts and evaluations are in English.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses that the benchmark can help develop next-generation multimodal AI assistants and track progress toward expert assistants. It also highlights risks related to voice imitation, including identity spoofing, harassment, fraud, impersonation, and privacy violations, and proposes consent, provenance, anti-impersonation safeguards, consent gating, watermarking or traceability, safety cards, and governance for auditing and removal.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors state that the benchmark may carry biases from its source data and design choices. Questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources, which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles and associated style prompts, which may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. The dataset is also primarily monolingual, with all prompts and evaluations in English except five Chinese roles.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes several limitations: the 10.5K-item dataset may still be limited in diversity; all prompts and evaluations are in English except five Chinese roles, limiting generalization to diverse linguistic settings; only a limited range of models was evaluated, with just one proprietary system; the evaluation methodology relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring that may introduce noise and bias; the benchmark may inherit biases from source data and design choices; the role-play subset may encode stereotypes or omit important personas; task coverage excludes video-audio integration and continuous audio-visual streaming; and the offline, static evaluation does not measure latency, partial utterance handling, interruption, or error recovery.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating voice assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing, and for facilitating future research on multimodal AI assistants. The paper explicitly states that the dataset is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating. It is intended for researchers to better evaluate voice assistants and support transparent, longitudinal assessment of system capabilities. The authors also prohibit training or releasing models intended to reproduce identifiable speakers without documented consent and require downstream users to implement consent gating and watermarking or traceability of synthetic audio.
